# Version Control with Git

Git is a version control system: it keeps a complete history of every change
you make to your files, and lets you step back to any earlier version
whenever you need to. If you've ever kept a folder full of files like
`code.R`, `code_v2.R`, `code_v2_final.R`,
`code_v2_final_ACTUALFINAL.R`, and `code_v2_final_ACTUALFINAL_revised.R`; you've already run into the problem Git solves.

Manually saving multiple copies of a file "just in case" is a fragile
system. It wastes storage, and worse, it's easy to lose track of which
version is actually the most recent, or to accidentally overwrite something
important. Git solves this by tracking a single copy of each file along with
a full history of every change made to it — you can always recover an
earlier version without needing separate saved copies cluttering your
project.

It's worth noting up front that Git is fundamentally a *local* tool: it runs
on your own computer and doesn't require an internet connection or an
account anywhere. The collaborative, multi-user features you may associate
with version control come from connecting Git to an external hosting
service — GitHub being the most common. This chapter focuses on using Git
locally; the next chapter covers GitHub and collaboration.

## Creating a GitHub account

Before diving into Git itself, you'll need a GitHub account, since we'll be
connecting your local repositories to GitHub throughout this course (and
you've likely already done this if you set up your course textbook repo).

If you don't already have one, go to <https://github.com> and click
**Sign up**. A few tips when creating your account:

- **Choose a professional username.** This will be visible on any public
  repositories you create, and often ends up on your resume or CV — think
  `firstname-lastname` or something similarly clean, rather than an old
  gamer tag or nickname.
- **Use an email address you'll have long-term access to.** Many students
  use their university email, but consider whether you'll still have access
  to it after graduating — a personal email is usually the safer long-term choice.
- **Free accounts are sufficient** for everything in this course. GitHub's
  free tier includes unlimited public and private repositories.

Once your account is created, you're ready to start using Git from the
command line and connecting it to GitHub.

## Command line basics

Git is typically used from the command line (Terminal on Mac, or Command
Prompt/PowerShell on Windows). If you haven't used a command line before,
know that it only takes a small set of commands to use Git comfortably.

When you open a terminal, you'll see a prompt — often a `$` on Mac/Linux or
a `>` on Windows — followed by a blinking cursor, waiting for input. When
copying commands from this book, only copy the part *after* the prompt
symbol, not the symbol itself.

Your terminal opens into a specific folder (your working directory), and
you navigate between folders using the `cd` ("change directory") command:

- Move into a subfolder: `cd Documents`
- Move up to the parent folder: `cd ..`
- Move to your home directory: `cd ~` (Mac/Linux) or `cd \` (Windows, moves
  to the root directory instead)

You can chain these together — for example, `cd ../..` moves up two levels
at once.

**Pro Tip: pasting a file path instead of typing it out.** Rather than typing
out a long path by hand (and risking a typo), you can drag and drop, or
copy and paste:

- **On Mac:** in Terminal, type `cd ` (with a trailing space, don't press
  Enter yet), then drag the folder from Finder directly into the Terminal
  window. It will automatically fill in the full path — press Enter to
  confirm. Alternatively, in Finder, hold **Option** and right-click the
  folder — the menu will show "Copy [name] as Pathname," which copies the
  full path to your clipboard so you can paste it directly after `cd `.
- **On Windows:** in File Explorer, navigate to the folder you want, then
  click into the address bar at the top and copy the path shown there. In
  Command Prompt, type `cd ` (with a trailing space), right-click to paste
  the path, and press Enter.

## Configuring Git

Before using Git for the first time, you need to tell it who you are. This
identity gets attached to every change you make, which matters once you
start collaborating with others. Run the following in your terminal,
substituting your own name and email:

```
git config --global user.name "First Last"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

The `--global` flag applies these settings to every Git repository on your
computer. Make sure you use your email address associated with your GitHub account.

To check your current configuration at any time:

```
git config --list
```

## Getting help

If you forget how a Git command works, you don't need to leave the
terminal. Any of the following will pull up documentation for a given Git
command (Git calls these "verbs"):

```
git help <verb>
git <verb> --help
```

For example, `git help commit` will explain everything the `commit` command
can do.

## Creating a repository

A **repository** (or "repo") is simply a folder that Git is tracking. To
turn an ordinary folder into a Git repository, you first need to navigate
into it in your terminal.

You can type out the path manually using `cd`, but an easier way (especially
on Mac) is to type `cd ` (with a trailing space, don't press Enter yet),
then drag the folder from Finder directly into the Terminal window — it
will automatically fill in the full path for you. Press Enter to confirm.

Once you're in the right folder, run:

```
git init
```

This creates a hidden `.git` subfolder, where Git stores all of its
version history — you don't need to look inside it or interact with it
directly, but its presence is what makes the folder a repository.

## Tracking files

Initializing a repository doesn't automatically start tracking the files
inside it — you have to tell Git which files to watch. Check what Git
currently sees with:

```
git status
```

This will list any untracked files. To start tracking a specific file:

```
git add filename.R
```

Or to track everything in the current folder at once:

```
git add .
```

Be thoughtful when using `git add .`, though. Git is built for tracking
plain-text files — scripts, RMarkdown documents, YAML files — where it can
meaningfully record what changed line by line. It doesn't handle binary
files (images, Word documents, Excel files) the same way, and large or
frequently-regenerated files can bloat your repository unnecessarily.
That's what `.gitignore` is for, covered next.

## Ignoring files

A `.gitignore` file tells Git which files or file types to never track,
even if someone runs `git add .`. This saves you from accidentally
tracking files you don't want cluttering your project history.

To create one, make a new plain-text file in your repository's top-level
folder named exactly `.gitignore` — no file extension, and note the leading
period. You can create this using any plain-text editor (TextEdit on Mac,
Notepad on Windows), or directly from RStudio via **File > New File > Text
File**, saving it as `.gitignore`.

A couple of things to watch for:

- **On Windows:** Notepad and File Explorer may refuse to let you name a
  file starting with a period, or may silently add a `.txt` extension. If
  this happens, create the file with any name first, then rename it in File
  Explorer — or use the RStudio method above, which avoids the issue
  entirely. You may also need to enable "File name extensions" in File
  Explorer's View tab to confirm the name saved correctly (it should read
  `.gitignore` with nothing after it).
- **On Mac:** make sure TextEdit doesn't add a hidden `.txt` extension
  behind the scenes — the file needs to be named `.gitignore`, not
  `.gitignore.txt`. Since it starts with a period, `.gitignore` is also a
  hidden file in Finder; you may need to enable "show hidden files"
  (Cmd+Shift+.) to see it after creating it.

A couple of things to watch for:

- Make sure your text editor doesn't add a hidden `.txt` extension behind
  the scenes — the file needs to be named `.gitignore`, not
  `.gitignore.txt`.
- Since it starts with a period, `.gitignore` is a hidden file. You may need
  to enable "show hidden files" in Finder (Cmd+Shift+.) to see it after
  creating it.

Some common candidates for `.gitignore` rules:

- **Binary files**, since Git can't meaningfully track changes within them
  (images, PDFs, Word/Excel files)
- **Code-generated files**, since anything a script can regenerate doesn't
  need its own tracked history (rendered HTML output, compiled figures)
- **Large files**, since they slow Git down — GitHub enforces a hard 100 MB
  limit per file, though if you're already excluding binary and
  code-generated files you'll rarely approach that

A `.gitignore` file uses pattern matching so you don't have to list every
file individually. For example:

```
*.jpg
*.png
*.docx
*.xlsx
figures/
manuscript_files/
.Rhistory
.Rproj.user/
```

The `*` wildcard means "any characters," so `*.jpg` excludes every `.jpg`
file at once. A trailing slash, like `figures/`, excludes an entire folder.

Most of the rules above target file *types* by extension — but the last two,
`.Rhistory` and `.Rproj.user/`, are specific files and folders that RStudio
generates automatically:

- `.Rhistory` is a file RStudio creates to log every command you've typed in
  the Console. It's a running record of your keystrokes, not something you
  write yourself, and it gets regenerated every time you use R — so there's
  no reason to track it.
- `.Rproj.user/` is a hidden folder RStudio creates to store your personal
  settings for an RStudio Project, like your window layout and which files
  were open. It's specific to your own computer, so tracking it wouldn't be
  useful to anyone else opening the project.

## The 3 states

Once a file is tracked by Git, it moves through three possible states:
**modified**, **staged**, and **committed**.

- A file is **modified** when you've made changes that Git hasn't recorded
  yet. The new version is saved on your computer, but Git doesn't know about it yet.
- **Staging** a file (`git add`) marks it as ready to be included in the
  next commit — think of this as building a list of changes you're about
  to save.
- **Committing** (`git commit`) takes everything currently staged and
  permanently records that snapshot in the file's history.

Note that `git add` serves two different purposes depending on the
situation: for a brand-new file, it tells Git to start tracking it for the
first time; for a file Git is already tracking, it stages your latest edits
so they're ready for the next commit. Either way, you only need to run the
command once — Git automatically knows which case applies.

To make a commit:

```
git commit -m "Short description of what changed"
```

Every commit needs a message (the `-m` flag), and it's worth taking that
seriously — a clear, specific message ("Fix heading levels in index.Rmd")
is far more useful to future-you than a vague one ("updates").

## Un-staging files

Sometimes you'll stage a file you didn't mean to — maybe you forgot to add
a rule to `.gitignore` first. To un-stage a file without committing it:

```
git rm --cached filename
```

This removes the file from the staging area but leaves it untouched on
your computer. Pattern matching works here too, but the wildcard needs a
backslash in front of it:

```
git rm --cached \*.jpg
```

## Recovering a previous version of a file

This is where Git's real power shows up. Because every commit is a
snapshot in time, you can always go back and retrieve an earlier version of
a file. Start by viewing your commit history:

```
git log
```

Each entry shows a commit message and a long string of letters and numbers
called a **hash**, which uniquely identifies that commit. Descriptive
commit messages pay off here — they make it much easier to scan the log
and recognize which commit you're looking for.

To restore a specific file to how it looked at a given commit:

```
git checkout <hash> -- filename.ext
```

## Removing Git

If you ever want to stop version-controlling a folder entirely — turning it
back into a regular, untracked folder — you can delete Git's hidden
tracking folder:

```
rm -rf .git
```

Use this with caution: it permanently discards the entire commit history
for that folder.

## Git everyday

Most of the commands in this chapter — configuring your identity,
initializing a repository, setting up `.gitignore` — are things you'll only
do once, or once per new project. In your regular day-to-day use of Git,
the commands you'll reach for constantly are just `git add` and
`git commit`. Everything else here is worth knowing, but you can always
come back to this chapter (or search online) when you need it.

## In-class Exercise: Practicing Git Basics

For this exercise, you'll create a small practice repository and put the
commands from this chapter to use. This is a local exercise — you won't
need GitHub yet (that's next chapter).

1. **Create a practice folder.** Somewhere on your computer (not inside your
   course-repo folder), create a new folder called `git-practice`.

2. **Initialize it as a Git repository.** Navigate into the folder in your
   terminal and run `git init`.

3. **Create a few files.** Inside `git-practice`, create two plain-text
   files: `notes.txt` (with a sentence or two of any text) and
   `data-summary.R` (an R script — a comment or two is fine, it doesn't need
   to run anything), and save them in the folder.

4. **Check Git's status.** Run `git status`. You should see both files
   listed as untracked.

5. **Start tracking your files and make your first commit.** Stage both
   files and commit them with a descriptive message.

6. **Create a `.gitignore` file.** Add a rule to ignore `.Rhistory` and
   `.Rproj.user/`, then create a dummy `.Rhistory` file in the folder to
   confirm — running `git status` afterward should show it's being ignored,
   not listed as untracked.

7. **Make an edit.** Open `notes.txt` and add a new sentence. Run
   `git status` again — notice how Git now describes this file differently
   than it did for a brand-new untracked file.

8. **Stage and commit the edit**, with a new commit message describing what
   changed.

9. **View your history.** Run `git log` and find the hash for your first
   commit.

10. **Recover the old version.** Use `git checkout <hash> -- notes.txt` to
    revert `notes.txt` back to its original content. Open the file to
    confirm the edit from step 7 is gone.

### What to submit in Canvas

Take a screenshot of your terminal after running `git log` (showing both
commits), and briefly describe (2–3 sentences) what happened when you
recovered the earlier version of `notes.txt` in step 10.
